name: Scratch
title: Scratch (3.0)

type.text: **There is no static type check**: A block accepts a value of any kind, and a mismatch appears only when the script runs
**No sum types**: An alternative is not a declared type; the script tests a value with an `if` or a sensing condition
**No generics**: A list block is not parameterised by an element type
**One flat namespace for message names**: Every message name is project-wide, so a name collision is a naming decision rather than a scope decision
**No null safety**: A variable that was never set reads as an empty value, and a block that needs a value can run with none
**No module boundary**: The project is one program, and a sprite exposes its blocks without a declared interface

construction.text: **Global mutable state is the default**: A variable created "for all sprites" is writable by every script in the project
**No immutability**: A value in a variable can be changed by any script that names it
**A sprite is a self-contained unit**: Costume, sound, and scripts live together, so one actor's behaviour is defined in one place
**The event model separates the trigger from the action**: The green flag, a key press, a sprite click, or a received message starts a script, and the script does not know who started it
**Cloning separates an instance from its definition**: `create clone of myself` copies a sprite's scripts at run time, so a repeated actor is written once
**A custom block is the only abstraction**: `define` gives a named sequence with inputs, and "run without screen refresh" is the one control over its granularity

memory.text: **The runtime owns every object**: No allocation and no deallocation block exists, and a sprite, a costume, or a clone is reclaimed automatically, so a script never names memory
**A clone can be deleted explicitly**: `delete this clone` bounds the number of live actors
**The clone count is the practical limit**: Scratch caps the number of clones, so a `forever` loop that clones without a `delete` reaches the cap rather than exhausting memory
**The media assets are the project's footprint**: Costumes, backdrops, and sounds dominate the size and the load time of a project

error.text: **There is no structured error path**: No exception and no error value exists, and a failed block simply does not produce the expected effect
**Nothing marks a failed operation**: A block that cannot do what it says leaves the value unchanged or produces a placeholder, and the script continues
**No composable result type**: A block returns one value, and no value can carry the fact that an operation failed
**The stage gives immediate feedback**: An out-of-stage sprite is visibly off-stage, and a sensing block can test for a touch
**Debugging is by observation**: There is no breakpoint, so the ordinary method is a variable monitor or a `say` block

concurrency.text: **Scripts are concurrent by default**: Every hat block in the project runs in parallel, and no script starts or joins another by hand
**A broadcast is global**: Any sprite can listen for any message, so a broadcast couples the sender to every listener in the project
**The scheduler is cooperative and single-threaded**: The scripts advance one after another within a frame, so an interleaved update does not arise in the middle of a block
**A clone runs its own copy of the script**: `when I start as a clone` gives each instance an independent thread of control
**A shared variable is updated by many scripts without a lock**: Correctness depends on where each script yields, which the programmer must reason about
**One frame is the unit of timing**: The green-flag scripts share the frame budget, so the loop rate is the scheduling contract

platform.text: **The runtime is the same on every target**: A project runs in the browser player and in the offline editor with the same blocks
**The sandbox bounds what a project can do**: A project reaches no file system and no network, so its effect is confined to the runtime
**MIT Media Lab maintains the runtime and the community site**: The editor, the player, and the sharing site come from one organisation
**The project file is an open document**: A `.sb3` project is a zip archive of JSON and assets, so a project can be read and converted
**Cloud variables are a hosted service**: They work only on the Scratch site, so a project that uses them depends on that host
**An extension changes the runtime's surface**: The Music, Pen, and video-sensing extensions, and the hardware extensions, add blocks the player must supply

performance.text: **The runtime executes the blocks directly**: The player holds the block scripts and runs them, so there is no build step between the editor and the running project
**"Run without screen refresh" removes the frame yield**: A custom block with that option runs to completion inside one frame, so a heavy computation can finish without waiting
**Turbo Mode removes the frame wait entirely**: The option runs the project as fast as the runtime allows
**Animation is capped near the redraw rate**: A loop yields each frame, so smooth motion is limited to the display rate
**A large script count degrades the frame**: Every script shares one frame budget, so the project slows as the script count and the clone count grow

ecosystem.text: **The ecosystem is the runtime and one community site**: The blocks, the media library, and the sharing site are the whole environment, and there is no general package manager
**The adoption in education is very large**: The project is used in K-12 classrooms worldwide
**A large public project corpus exists**: Shared and remixed projects are a huge body of worked examples
**The media and sprite libraries are built in**: Backdrops, costumes, and sounds ship with the editor
**Third-party players and add-ons are the extension point**: TurboWarp, Scratch Addons, and the extension gallery live outside the official editor

evolution.text: **The project format carries a version and a converter**: An older project is converted when it is opened in the current editor
**MIT maintains the editor as a product**: The runtime, the editor, and the site receive continuing updates
**The offline editor mirrors the online one**: A project runs without a connection to the site
**A block set can change between editor releases**: A removed or renamed block can leave an older project needing an edit

domain.text: **The domain is one thing: teaching programming to beginners**: The design goal is computational thinking, and everything outside it is out of scope
**It is not usable for a production application**: There is no file access, no network, no performance target, and no general library
**The classroom fit is exemplary**: Drag-and-drop, immediate feedback, and shareable projects match the teaching case
**It is the first language in many curricula**: The adoption in schools is the evidence for the fit
**The move to a text language is the known gap**: A learner must leave Scratch to continue, and the transfer is not automatic

learning.text: **The curve is effectively zero**: The interface is drag-and-drop, and there is no syntax to learn
**The block shape prevents the syntax error**: A block that does not fit cannot be placed
**The stage returns immediate feedback**: One click runs the project and shows the result
**The ceiling is low for a capable learner**: After the core blocks there is little further depth
**"Run without screen refresh" is the one advanced idea**: A heavy custom block must use it to finish inside a frame

syntax.text: **The syntax is the block shape**: An invalid nesting is impossible, because the editor accepts only a shape that fits
**The expression blocks nest visually**: An operator block occupies an input slot, so the precedence is explicit without parentheses
**The blocks are named in the reader's language**: The editor localises the labels and the variable names
**A small computation becomes a tall column of blocks**: The notation is compact per block and long per expression
**There is no text form in the editor**: A script cannot be typed, searched, or diffed as text

testing.text: **There is no test framework**: No assertion and no runner exists, so a test is a manual run
**An error appears only when a script runs**: A wrong block is found by executing the project
**The stage is a built-in observation harness**: Motion, sound, and `say` show the program state directly
**A variable monitor exposes a value on the stage**: Any variable can be shown and watched as it changes
**Verification is by inspection**: The programmer checks the result by watching the project, not by a repeatable check

security.text: **A project runs in a sandbox**: No block opens a file or a socket, so a project reaches no file system and no network and its effect is confined to the runtime
**The runtime is the same for every project**: A shared project cannot ship a native binary
**A cloud variable is shared global state**: Every player of the project can write it, so a project that trusts it can be misled
**The community features are moderated, not secured**: The safety of the sharing site is a policy of the site, not a property of the language
**A third-party player can add an unsafe surface**: An alternative player or an add-on can extend the runtime beyond the sandbox

tradeoffs: **Visual blocks trade expressiveness for legibility**: The block shape carries the nesting rule, so a syntax error is not expressible — which is the design goal
**The block vocabulary is deliberately small**: A small instruction set is the pedagogy, not an oversight
**The actor-based organisation mirrors the stage**: A project is organised by sprite because the program is a scene
**The educational scope is a scope decision**: The absence of files, network, and performance is the boundary of the design
**Sharing and remixing are community choices**: The remix model is a policy of the site, not a property of the language
**Turbo Mode is an optional accelerator**: It removes the frame wait, and the choice is the user's
verdict: Scratch's design yields moderate core coupling, and the marks fall where the pedagogy put them. Global variables are the project namespace, a broadcast reaches every sprite, and there is no type check, no structured error path, and no module boundary; the constrained environment keeps the consequence small. The visual block model removes the syntax error entirely, the event model separates a trigger from the action it starts, and a sprite is a self-contained unit. Main strengths: a zero learning curve, an exemplary classroom fit, very large K-12 adoption, and a sandbox that bounds what a project can do. Main weaknesses: it is not usable for a production application, the domain is a single one, the block vocabulary is shallow, and testing is by inspection.

energy.text: Runs on a virtual machine, above native code in the energy and time benchmarks [@pereira2017energy]; a causal re-analysis attributes most of the gap to execution time [@vankempen2025green].

ai-readiness.text: Sparse training data: models write it unreliably [@joel2025lowresource].

safety.text: No certified or standards-qualified path for safety-critical systems.
